definition: A single-celled prokaryotic microorganism lacking a membrane-bound nucleus, found in nearly every environment on Earth.
A single-celled prokaryote genetically and biochemically distinct from bacteria, often found in extreme environments.
A microscopic infectious agent that replicates only inside the living cells of a host organism.
An organism, such as a bacterium or archaeon, whose cell lacks a membrane-bound nucleus.
An organism whose cells contain a membrane-bound nucleus, including fungi, protozoa, algae, plants, and animals.
Any microorganism capable of causing disease in a host.
A substance, often produced by microorganisms, that kills or inhibits the growth of bacteria.
The ability of a microorganism to survive exposure to a drug that would normally kill it or stop its growth.
A bacterium that retains crystal violet stain due to a thick peptidoglycan cell wall, appearing purple under a microscope.
A bacterium with a thin peptidoglycan layer and outer membrane that does not retain crystal violet stain, appearing pink.
A dormant, highly resistant structure formed by certain bacteria to survive extreme conditions.
A whip-like appendage used by some microorganisms for movement.
A hair-like surface appendage on some bacteria used for attachment or DNA transfer during conjugation.
A structured community of microorganisms adhering to a surface, encased in a self-produced protective matrix.
A metabolic process that converts sugars into acids, gases, or alcohol without requiring oxygen.
Describes an organism or process that requires oxygen.
Describes an organism or process that occurs without oxygen.
An organism that thrives in physically or chemically extreme conditions, such as high heat, acidity, or salinity.
An organism that grows optimally at high temperatures, often above 45C.
An organism that thrives in environments with very high salt concentrations.
A close, long-term biological interaction between two different organisms.
A symbiotic relationship in which both participating organisms benefit.
A molecule produced by a pathogen that contributes to its ability to cause disease.
A poisonous substance produced by a living organism, capable of causing disease when introduced into a host.
A toxin secreted by a microorganism into its surrounding environment.
A toxic component of the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria, released when the cell is destroyed.
A biological preparation that stimulates the immune system to recognize and fight a specific pathogen.
A molecule capable of triggering an immune response, often found on the surface of a pathogen.
A protein produced by the immune system that recognizes and binds to a specific antigen.
A laboratory technique used to exponentially amplify a specific segment of DNA.
The complete set of genetic material of an organism.
The process of determining the complete order of nucleotides in an organism's DNA.
A small, circular piece of DNA in bacteria that replicates independently of the chromosomal DNA.
The movement of genetic material between organisms other than by reproduction from parent to offspring.
A process by which bacteria transfer genetic material directly through cell-to-cell contact.
The uptake and incorporation of free DNA from the environment by a bacterial cell.
The transfer of bacterial DNA from one cell to another by a bacteriophage.
A change in an organism's DNA sequence, which can arise spontaneously or from environmental exposure.
A virus that infects and replicates specifically within bacteria.
A nutrient-containing substance used to grow microorganisms in a laboratory.
A shallow, flat-lidded dish used to culture microorganisms on solid growth medium.
A process that eliminates all forms of microbial life from a surface or substance.
A heat treatment process that kills most harmful microorganisms in a liquid, such as milk, without fully sterilizing it.
A device that uses pressurized steam to sterilize laboratory equipment and materials.
The technique of using instruments to view objects too small to be seen by the naked eye.
A microscope that uses a beam of electrons to achieve much higher magnification than light microscopes.
The scientific practice of classifying organisms into hierarchical groups based on shared characteristics.
The standardized two-part naming system for species, consisting of genus and species names.
The basic unit of biological classification, generally defined as a group of organisms capable of interbreeding.
A taxonomic rank grouping closely related species.
A major taxonomic rank grouping organisms that share a broad body plan or genetic lineage.
The highest rank in biological classification, dividing all life into Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya.
A component of the bacterial and archaeal ribosome whose gene sequence is widely used to determine evolutionary relationships.
The study of genetic material recovered directly from environmental samples, without isolating individual organisms.
The collective community of microorganisms living in a particular environment, such as the human gut.
A live microorganism that, when consumed in adequate amounts, provides a health benefit to the host.
An infectious disease that can be transmitted from animals to humans.
A sudden increase in the number of disease cases beyond what is normally expected in a population.
An epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents.
A sudden occurrence of disease cases in a specific place or population.
The time between exposure to a pathogen and the appearance of symptoms.
An infection acquired within a hospital or healthcare setting.
The practice of preventing infection by inhibiting the growth of microorganisms on living tissue.
The process of eliminating most microorganisms on a non-living surface.
A set of four criteria used to establish that a specific microorganism causes a specific disease.
The scientific theory that many diseases are caused by microorganisms.
A disproven historical theory that living organisms could arise from non-living matter.
An organism that obtains energy by oxidizing inorganic compounds rather than through photosynthesis or organic matter.
The process by which certain microorganisms convert atmospheric nitrogen into a form usable by plants.
A bacterial and archaeal immune defense system, adapted into a widely used tool for precise gene editing.
A bacterial protein that cuts DNA at specific sequences, originally part of a defense against viruses.
DNA formed by combining genetic material from different sources.
A theory proposing that mitochondria and chloroplasts originated from free-living bacteria engulfed by ancestral eukaryotic cells.
An informal grouping for eukaryotic organisms, including protozoa and algae, that are not classified as animals, plants, or fungi.
The scientific study of fungi.
The scientific study of viruses.
The scientific study of bacteria.
